summary: Announces that RFC numbers can now be obtained on-line through NLS at OFFICE-1 instead of at SRI-ARC, though one can still phone the NIC. It also notes that pre-assigned journal numbers work only on the system they came from.

plainLanguage.summary: To get a number for a new note you now use a different computer, or just call. Reserved numbers only work where they were reserved.

questions: how were rfc numbers assigned early
subtitle: Announcement of changes to where and how RFC numbers were assigned on the network

tldr.problem: The early network needed a way to assign unique numbers to RFC documents, and procedures for getting these numbers needed to change as systems were reorganized.
tldr.mechanism: RFC numbers can now be obtained online through NLS at OFFICE-1 instead of through SRI-ARC, though telephone requests to the NIC continue to be accepted.
tldr.outcome: The change moved the distribution mechanism but kept the numbering system operational during the transition between network resource centers.

today: RFC 628 is a meta-announcement from March 1974 about procedures for obtaining RFC numbers and journal numbers in the early network.

sections.title: Moving RFC Number Assignment
sections.content:
In the early ARPANET, Request for Comments documents needed unique numbers, assigned by a central authority. This RFC announces that the online system for obtaining RFC numbers has moved from SRI-ARC to a different location: OFFICE-1.

Authors can still obtain numbers online through the new system, or they may continue to telephone the Network Information Center (NIC) directly if they prefer not to use the online facilities.
sections.plainLanguage: The place where you could ask for a number online moved to a different computer. Or you could keep calling to ask for one.

sections.title: Pre-assigned Journal Numbers
sections.content: The RFC also notes that pre-assigned journal numbers (other than RFC numbers themselves) can only be used through NLS on the specific system from which they were taken. This restriction prevents confusion and maintains control over number assignment across the distributed network.
sections.plainLanguage: Reserved numbers you get from one computer only work on that same computer, not on others.

sections.title: Getting a Number
sections.content: Authors had two methods to obtain an RFC number: use the online system at OFFICE-1 through NLS, or call the Network Information Center directly by telephone. Both methods provide the same result: a unique number for a new RFC document. The choice between them is left to the author's preference and access to systems.
sections.plainLanguage: You could pick a method that worked for you: the online computer or the phone call.
